projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with George Harsch, Jr. was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of Veteran George Harsch, Junior. Mr. Harsch had served in the U.S. Navy during World War II at Korea. During World War II he served in the Pacific Theater, and his highest rank was lieutenant. I'm Tom Swope. And this recording was made at Mr. Harsch's home in Chesterland, Ohio, on September 27th, 2001. George was 76 at the time of this recording. Where did you live during then when the war started?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: In Cleveland on Hamlen Avenue. That's--you're talking World War II, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's the one.

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That's what we're here to talk about today.

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: And everybody remembers where they were on Pearl Harbor Day, right? I was in the Sea Scouts at that time, and another Sea Scout and I were out looking for a location to hold a dinner dance. And so he and I were out riding around in his car looking for this place, and when we had the radio on we heard about Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: I don't remember exactly any specific reaction, but I knew it was serious. And I--I had a vague idea where Pearl Harbor was, but I didn't know for sure where it was. As more people came on the radio and were talking about it I knew that it really was serious and that something was going to be going on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you tempted to run out and sign up the next day?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: No. Never even considered that I don't think. But I think the following--I think it was the following summer the Coast Guard invited the Sea Scouts to ride on the Coast Guard Cutter in Cleveland here. That was the Tahoma, as I remember. And we went from Cleveland over to Put-in-Bay and came back over Saturday, Sunday. And I can remember vaguely sort of wishing that the Tahoma would get orders to go to sea and do something because we were already aboard and we figured they'd take us with us--with them and we'd participate then. But I had no inclination to get into the service or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: When I was a senior in high school, I went to East Tech, and I graduated in May of '43. But sometime in early '43 they had a test at school. And this was a test to see if you wanted to become an officer in the Army or Navy. There were two tests given. One was for the Army, and that was called the A-12. And the other was for the Navy, and that was the V-12. And I passed the tests. So I graduated in about the third week of May, and--but I was already sworn in to the Navy in about the first week of May. So I actually was in before I graduated, and I was just 17 at the time. So my first active duty station was to go to school. So I received orders to report to Baldwin-Wallace College I think the 1st of July in 1943. And there we--I think there were 350 of us. Most of us were right out of high school. But some of the people reporting were men that had already been to sea and they qualified for the V-12 program while they were at sea. And so then they were transferred back. There were a number of V-12 units around the country. I don't know how many there were totally. But we went to Baldwin-Wallace. So for the rest of '43 and then up until about October of '44 we were in some pretty intensive education. We were taking the regular civilian courses plus Navy courses. And we took astronomy, and Naval history, and Navy orientation. And there was a push on physical conditioning, and we'd be out every morning at 6:30, rain or shine, snow, or whatever. And we'd be out in the street exercising, and then we'd have to run around the block. And then we'd go in and get cleaned up, shaved, showered, and whatnot for breakfast right at school. So after I left BW I went to--I was transferred to Asbury Park, and that was billed as a midshipmen school or pre-midshipmen school, and I was there a couple months, and then transferred to Columbia University for midshipmen school. And I went to Columbia I think it was December 27th of '44. And we were at Columbia until we graduated in early April of '45. And then I--when I graduated I received--I got my commission, and I became an ensign, and then I was given a duty station aboard an LSM. And the LSM was located in Hawaii, so I had to fly to Hawaii. No, I didn't fly. I had to go to San Francisco and pick up a transport that was going to Hawaii. And so I did that and picked up my ship there. And it had a load of cargo for--it was an LSM. It had a load of cargo for Okinawa. So we--from Pearl Harbor from Hawaii we went to Okinawa. And we got there in time for a lot of the mop-up operations. And we primarily anchored in Buckner Bay. And we had a smoke generator aboard. And they used a bunch of the LSMs on one edge of the bay. We generated smoke, and then the smoke covered the whole bay. Because the kamikazes were coming in every night, and we tried to distract them and to cover the fleet with the smoke so that they couldn't see clearly as to what they were doing.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What does LSM stand for?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Landing ship medium, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your unit at that time?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Amphibious Forces Pacific Fleet.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Okay. Did it have a numerical designation or anything?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: It probably had, but I don't remember what it was now.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So did you go ashore at all in Okinawa?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: No, I don't think so. I don't remember going ashore there at all. What I do remember is not too long after we were there I can remember sitting up almost all night at general quarters because the kamikazes were coming over. And since we were the ones that were making smoke that left us sort of exposed for any attack. We did anchor by the stern anchor so that the smoke blew over us, but it didn't get to be full and billowing until it got a little farther away. And then--I think it did a pretty effective job of covering the fleet with smoke. But the big thing I remember is--and I think a lot of people will remember the big storm, the hurricane, and everybody had to go to sea. And those seas were monstrous. I had never seen such a flotter. When we were on the conning we had a duty station where the officer of the deck stayed up on the top of the conning tower and had a couple men with him, signalman and a lookout, and the top of the conning tower was, oh, probably 30 feet or 40 feet off of the water. And one time you'd look out and you were even with the water. Another time you'd look out and the water was 50, 60 feet down. So there were--there were some pretty big waves, and we got through it. The ship was like a cork bobbing around out there. And, of course, we had to be in a formation so that we had the Navy ships protecting us around the outer flanks and whatnot. And station keeping, trying to keep your place in line and your place looking at the people abreast of you was very difficult because those waves were throwing you all over the place. And everybody, of course, was having the same problem. And it got to be such a problem that they suggested we turn our running lights on, which was very unusual because during war time you didn't display any lights because of Japanese submarine attack possibilities. So we turned the running lights on, and that made it a lot easier to follow. Of course we didn't expect anybody would attack us in that kind of weather.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any ships in your group?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: No. I don't think so. An LSM has an open tank deck, and we had sections of pontoon barges, and that was our cargo going to Okinawa. But there was a couple other--one other LSM that I know of had bags of cement on their--in their deck. And the kamikazes came in and hit the cement and didn't damage the ship hardly at all. Made a big flash, you know, and burned some paint off, but it didn't really hurt anything.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you ever have any very close encounters with kamikazes?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: No. Uh-uh.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Fortunately.

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: No. I just remember sitting there at night staying awake all night, trying to stay awake all night, waiting. Making smoke and waiting for something to happen. So from there we went to Guam, and that's when they started--the war in Europe was over about that time. No, that's--I'm getting mixed up.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The war ended about in May, early May, in Europe.

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: '45, yeah. I'm still in '44. So we went to--we bounced all over the Pacific and went to Guam, and Saipan, and Tinian, and Marcus Island. And that--that part's just kind of vague. But I remember going back to Guam and everybody was talking about points to go home because you--for certain duties and certain lengths of time you received points, and when you got up to a certain number of points, why, you were eligible to go home. Well, everybody had been on this ship from when it was built in Chicago, it was built at the Pullman Car Company, the people that make Pullman cars for trains. They built the LSM. And then it went down the Mississippi River and over to Hawaii. So they had all been on the ship for quite some time. So they had accumulated a lot more points than I had. So I was transferred off. And they went back to the states, and I stayed in Guam. And that's when I was put aboard an LCT. That's a landing craft utility. And I was the officer in charge, and I had a crew of about 12 men. And what we did was go out in the harbor alongside a cargo ship and pick up whatever cargo they had for the beach. And they'd load it on our deck, and we'd take it in. Most of the time we were able to go into a dock and unload. So we did that quite a bit. And then we also assisted in taking personnel that were going home. We'd put them on the tank deck and take them out to the transports that were loading up and heading back to the states. So we did that for quite a while. And I liked Guam. It was--it was a good duty station. And the food was--we got it off of the--from the base there. And we had one--one cook aboard the ship, and he was a real go-getter. And I can remember asking me one day, Skipper, I'm going over to get some bread. We were tied up alongside a cargo ship. And the cargo ship was operated by Merchant Marine. And they had some pretty nice living aboard those ships. And so he went aboard and got acquainted with the baker in the galley, and he came back aboard with six loaves of bread, and a couple of heads of lettuce, and some ice cream. Oh, and some milk. So we thought that was pretty good, because those were things we--we would have bread if he made it, but he didn't like to bake bread. So he and I had an agreement that if he could get bread someplace else is it okay if he didn't bake it. I said okay. So.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, were you involved at all in the preparations for the possible invasion of Japan?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, I think all of this was preparation for that. But with the activities at Okinawa I think things ended a lot sooner. And when the Battleship Missouri went in to Tokyo into the harbor there to effect the surrender we went up to a little island in the middle of the Pacific, as I remember it's sort of a triangular shape, and it was a mile by a mile and a half. And this was Marcus Island. And they had a pretty big radar installation there. And we went up there and effected the surrender of that island. They came aboard the--a destroyer that was with us, and they did the surrender on the destroyer the same day, same time as they were surrendering on the Missouri in Tokyo Bay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember when you heard the news that they had dropped the first bomb?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. Couldn't--couldn't really visualize what that was. But the--the--definitely the news coming over the radio was that this was going to end the war. Fine. That's good. Now I can go home, right? But it was still a few more months before I came home. So then they came home, and I went back to Baldwin-Wallace starting again in July of '46. So I think I came home in June of '46 then started back to school in July. And I finished up and got my degree there and then went to work and met my wife at work. And I always was interested in the submarines. And the sub was down at the 9th Street, and so I joined the reserves and trained on the submarine. And went to New London, Connecticut, on one vacation to go into that big tank where you go down 100 feet and you wear the Momson Lung and you escape the submarine from going up the rope with the knots in it. And I did that. And I had--the following year I had orders to go to Key West to qualify in submarines. And we were going to go there with a good friend of mine that lived up in Huron. In fact, he and I were roommates at Baldwin-Wallace in the V-12 program. And we were ready to go to Key West when orders came through to active duty. So in January, I think it was January '51 when I got recalled, and I went out to San Diego for a couple of weeks of reorientation. And then I was sent up to Seattle to get a what used to be an LCT, and they now changed the designater, they were called LSUs, landing ship utility. And had to get one of those out of mothballs and train the crew. And so we proceeded to do that. And while I was there I called home, talked to my wife one night. And she said, Can you find an apartment there? And I said, No, things are really jammed up. But I told her I'd go over and check with housing again the next day. And I went over, and, believe it or not, the lady had an apartment for me. So we--I told her, well, come on out. And we rented that apartment. So this complicated things because I didn't have a car. So I had to go out and buy a car. So I--I bought a 1934 Ford. That's the kind that had the front doors that opened. They call them suicide doors. And, but it was a good car. And we--I used that for transportation from the apartment over to the base when we outfitted the ship and got it all ready. So one kind of an interesting incident, the day I reported to the Bremerton Naval Shipyard I had to report in to the commander, the base commander, base captain, and he was aboard the Battleship Indiana. And I--I was there having lunch I think on the Indiana, and a messenger handed me a note. Said base captain wants to see you. And so we go see the base captain. And he said, Welcome aboard. I've got good news for you. Your cook is in jail. And he's got a trial coming up this afternoon. And the charge was drunken and disorderly. So somehow or other I got a ride into town where the court was going on. And I was to be a character witness for my cook that I had never met before. And he was standing before the judge. And I got there and--and he said, Do you represent this man? And I said, Yes, sir. I just reported aboard today, and this is my--the first thing that I have to do is participate in this. He said, Well, you've got your work cut out for you. He said, I'm just going to let this man go, and he'll be in your custody. So that's how I met my cook. And--but he was a good cook. But boy, did he like to drink. So from there we got the ship outfitted, and we moved down to San Diego. They put three LSUs in a what they called a LSD, landing ship dock. It's a--a dry dock that ballasts down and it has its own power. So it--and it--it goes pretty good speed. It probably makes 9, 9 to 12 knots, whereas the LSUs were good for about 5 and a half or 6 knots downhill. And, you know, there's no downhill on the ocean. So anyhow, we got orders to board this LSD. And he ballasted down and took us. But I didn't know exactly what do with the car, and I wasn't able to sell it real fast. So I just put it aboard the ship. I had one of the shipyard cranes just set it on the tank deck. And that's how we got it down to San Diego. And when we got down there I just--we came out of the LSD, and I just went over and beached it, dropped the bow ramp and drove it off. So we had that transportation in San Diego. In that year, in 1951, my wife was with me. We were married about a year or a year and a half at the time, and we lived in seven different apartments. Because we lived in the apartment in Bremerton. We got one apartment in San Diego, and then moved to a little better apartment in San Diego. Then we got orders to go to the Long Beach Naval Shipyard for some alterations to the ship, and we had to rent an apartment there. So we went up there. And then back down to San Diego. And I think it was at that point when they--they took the officers off of the LSU. There was only one officer on the LSU, and he was the skipper. They took the officers off and put a chief boatswain's mate in charge of the vessel. And so they put me then on the squadron staff, the LSU squadron staff. And there were two--two LSU squadrons. One was in San Diego. The other one was in Japan, Yokosuka, Japan. And idea was to move crews. We had 24, I don't remember the quantity now, but either 24 or 36 LSUs in San Diego, and probably 20 or 24 in Yokosuka. And out of Yokosuka we'd bring them in, we'd get them fixed up if they had any battle damage or any damage to them. Resupply them. Put a new crew on and send them over to Inchon or wherever they were needed in Korea. And so that was a--a 7 day a week job. That was 7 days, 24 hours a day. And kept us really busy. So I was the administrative officer in the squadron, and it was my job to schedule the crews, and the ships, and stuff like that. It was interesting time. And my wife and I, we treated it as a two-year vacation. So then I was transferred from squadron 1, no, I was first in squadron 3. I was transferred to squadron 1, which meant I had to go to Japan. Squadron 3 was in San Diego. Well, I went to Japan and became the advent officer for squadron 1. And I was there about two months and squadron 1 got transferred back to San Diego. And 3 went to Yokosuka. And that worked out pretty good. Then we got on a rotation thing, six months in the states and six months in Yokosuka. And so I finished up my two years in the Korean War in Japan, and I flew home from there on a Flying Tiger airplane. And it had a few seats up in the forward part of the cabin, but the back end of the cabin was all cargo, tie downs, and stuff like that. So that was--and these were still piston aircraft, and, you know, they didn't go that fast. So it took, oh, I think 40, if I remember correctly, it took like 42 hours to get to San Francisco from Yokosuka or Tokyo. I--we left from Tokyo. But we had to stop en route. We had to stop at Guam for refueling. And we had to stop at either Midway or Wake. And then we got to Honolulu, and we fueled up there and then took off for San Francisco. Each leg was about 12 or 14 hours. So, it was--that was a long time. And, you know, no beds or anything. You just sat in that chair and doze off when you have to. And one point we were going from Tokyo to Guam, and four engines, one engine coughed a little bit, and boy, everybody just startled and sat up and wondering, what's going on? Didn't want to see that happening over the ocean. But it kept going. We did all right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Backtracking a second to World War II, do you remember getting the news about F.D.R.'s death?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. I think we were saddened by that. Yeah. I don't remember any special services or anything like they do now. But everybody wondered what was going to happen and who was this guy Truman, you know. He sells hats. Okay. He's going to run the country.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any celebrations for either V-E or V-J Day?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. I remember--I don't remember exactly where we were, probably at Guam, when the war was declared over. And this was before we had to go to Marcus Island to, you know, get the official surrender. And I--I can remember people with Very pistols shooting things up in the air and that sort of thing. Then after a while you started getting newspapers and things like that, and you saw what was going on in New York and at Times Square, you know, where everybody was having such a big time, and you get a little jealous because we weren't having that big a time. It was fine that the war was over, but we weren't having any real big celebrations. But that's all right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you--what did the kind of things did you do for entertainment when you were over there?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Generally when the LSUs tied up in the harbor by the dock there would be more than one, or two, or three. There might be eight or 10. And the officers would all get together in--in one of our quarters, and we'd probably--we'd play bridge. I can remember there--this was at Saipan, and I can remember they had a dance. The base had a dance, and they invited any officers from the ships in the harbor to the officer's club for this dance. And it was kind of interesting, because as you came in you had to check your side arms. So here's this wall with all these 45s hanging on it. It just reminded me of the old Wild West, you know. And--but dance, no way you could dance, because there were a few nurses and the rest were guys. And so we didn't do much dancing. They had, if I remember correctly they had good food. Probably had plenty of beer and booze. So partied that way.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any USO shows come through?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: None--none of the real famous people like Bob Hope. There were some lesser people. And that was the good part about being tied up in--at the dock in Guam, because you could go to the movies on the base. We didn't have any movies aboard our ship, but you could go over to the base movies. And we went to the movies every night. And then once in a while they'd have some of the lesser-known USO people would be putting on a show. But most of the time we were just hanging around the ship and being ready. Because you--if you got orders you really didn't have too much time to get ready. You had to be ready all the time, you know. I remember at Guam we did--there was some bowling. Bowling alley there where--and I think they had the--the pins were all set by hand. They had the boys from Guam back in the pit there setting the pins up. Of course there was a lot of gambling, a lot of poker games you could get into, a lot of crap games. But I kind of stayed away from that stuff. I've never sat crap in my life. I played some poker. But don't even know how to use the dice.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: As you look back on the World War II experience does one thing come to mind as your most vivid memory of that?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: That typhoon where we had to put to sea from Buckner Bay. That--that was a real experience with those big waves. Your--the ship is like a cork, because you're hogging and sagging, you know, and the bow goes up, and the back end goes up, and the ship's going like this. You can hear the bulkheads warping and buckling. And--but the thing, the ship held together real well. I was surprised at that. Nothing, nothing real outstanding stands out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Didn't Halsey go through a couple of typhoons with his fleet?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, he probably did.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Seems like he had bad luck every time he--

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. I was impressed with some of the ships that came from Iwo Jima. They--they took a real beating there because they didn't have a good harbor to anchor in. There was essentially you just anchored off the island and they were at sea. And they, you know, tie--tie up to each other. And I can remember the skin on the ship is only, you know, quarter inch steel. And I can remember all the ribs on the ship because they were banging against each other all the time. And they--they were really beat up when they came off of there. Ours didn't get beat like that too much.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything else you can think of?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: I remember one day I--I told you about this cook, kind of in a courtroom in Seattle. Well, he was the first cook. And he straightened out a little bit. And, like I said, he was a real good cook. But he liked to drink. But he was transferred off to another ship, and I--I got another cook. And I got him right out of the hospital. He had been in--on one of the LSUs in Korea, and he bought some alcohol from a civilian in Korea, and it was wood alcohol. And it--I don't know what it did to his system, but for a while he went blind, and they were able to restore some of his sight. And that's--that's pretty nasty stuff. And then I had another cook. And we had morning muster one day, this was in San Diego, and we had morning muster, and the cook was missing. Anybody seen him? No. Nobody knows where he is. And this cook was, he was kind of a loner. And--but he buddied around with a guy from one of the other LSUs. And so I went over to see the skipper of the other LSU, and he had one man that was--that was gone. So about 9:30 in the morning I got called up to the office, the squadron office. They had received word from I don't know what agency, but my cook was in jail. This other guy's seaman was in jail. And they had been in the house of ill repute, and somebody shot and killed the janitor. So here we are. And, of course, Mexico, this all happened in Tijuana. And Mexico would not release these people because they were there in the house when the guy was shot, and they were holding them all as material witnesses, or as suspects, or whatever. But after, oh, about five or six days, maybe a week, he was released and came back aboard the ship. But he--he straightened out pretty fast. After that he--he didn't go anywhere. He stayed on the ship, and he'd read comic books or something like that. Then there was another guy. He was a seaman aboard my ship. And he buddied around with a guy from another ship, and they went ashore. And they--I guess the first thing that they do when they go ashore is find the nearest bar. And had a couple of drinks. So he and this other guy got drunk, and they stole a car. Took it over to Tijuana and tried to sell it. Well, lots of people frown on that type of activity. So I never saw him again. He was--he and the other man were arrested, and by I think the FBI, anyhow, one of the government agencies, and for theft and attempted foreign commerce of a stolen vehicle. So, you know, this brings lots of years, like 15 or 20 years. So it's--it's a really a study in personalities when you get a dozen people thrown together like that and the way they can live together and what happens. While I'm thinking of this, there's another incident that comes to mind. We got--this is out in Guam, and we got orders to go alongside the one AKA cargo ship, and three Marines came down, got on the ship at the dock, and said that they were going to go with us. And I said, Why do we want you to go with us? He says, We're going to guard the cargo. Hum, okay. What kind of cargo is it? Well, we didn't know, you know. All we knew is we were supposed to go pick it up. So we went alongside, and they had the cargo nets. And they were unloading cases of beer. Well, this--this ship's 105 feet long and 34 feet wide. You--you can get a lot of beer in that space. And we were built to be able to carry five tanks. So you can imagine the size of the tank deck. And they filled that up with beer. Well, of course, it's my responsibility to make sure that the cargo gets from the ship to the shore and gets unloaded. And in the mean time we're under the Marine guard so that nothing can happen. And, so, you know, I told the men, I said, don't even go near that beer because you'll be in bad trouble. Well, everything went fine. I went into galley for breakfast, and the cook says, Skipper, do you want a beer? And I said, Where did you get beer? You're not supposed to have beer on the ship. Oh, you remember we got that load of beer yesterday? Yeah, but that was under guard. He said, Oh, well. We managed to get some. I don't know how, or why, or where, but even under the Marine guard they were able to get three or four cases of beer and stash it away someplace. So you talk about American ingenuity, that's--that's it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Marines must have some beer too, right?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. They may have been a part of it. But a lot of things like that went on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: I think that just about does it, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right. Let's go.

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: While I was in Guam as the officer in charge of this LCT we got temporary orders to--one other LCT and I, Howard Mitchell, he was from Pennsylvania, was the skipper of the other one. So the two of us went to--took our ships to--and we were escorted. We went to Truk. This was after the war. And Truk was a pretty big--it's in Ito in the Pacific. And it's a pretty big Japanese installation. They had a lot of stuff there. Air bases, and resupplies for aircraft carriers, and things of that sort. And what they had done is they went to some island someplace, I don't remember which island, but they--they enslaved a bunch of people, brought them over to Truk, and had them growing vegetables and stuff like that on Truk. And with the war over there was a group of English or Australians that wanted to repatriate these people that the Japanese had brought in. So--so we met up with an Australian major that was handling this thing. And what we did is we had to first go over to where these people were. And the--the chief was a big guy. He had hands on him like that big. And we sat around in the woods in sort of powwow fashion, but they had logs or something for us to sit on, and we were to discuss how we could get these people onto this English transport. And that's where the LCTs came in, because we could go in and beach and take them out to the ship. And so a couple things that I remember about the meeting, we just talked in general terms about what we could do. But while we were doing this he clapped his hands, and two boys came running over. And he talked to them in whatever their language was, and they disappeared. Pretty soon they come back with six coconuts. And the chief took his machete and went shooo (ph) like that and cut the coconuts and handed us each a coconut so we could drink the milk out of it. That was interesting. But the big thing was, I told my wife about this before, the Japanese didn't provide any clothing for these people. So they were practically down to bare skin. And so the--there was also a Swiss missionary in this conversation. The Australian major, the swiss missionary, the chief, and Mitchell and I, and I think one other person. But anyhow, they asked what could we do about clothing for the women. And did we have any cloth. Well, we didn't really have very much cloth. But I went back to the ship and told the guys that, you know, if they have any extra clothing that they can spare that these women would like to wear the clothing while they're on the transports, see. So I took the--I had two or three bedspreads from my bed. And these are Navy bedspreads that are blue and grey striped, but right in the center is the Navy insignia. It says United States Navy, and it's got an anchor. And it's a circle about that big. And most of the guys had sheets, or extra T-shirts, and things of that sort. And so we gathered up quite a bit of stuff and gave it to the Australian major, and he took it over. And--and just a matter of one day I think is what it was, maybe it was two days. When we went over there to pick them up these people were all dressed. They were wearing this stuff. And I got a big kick out of this one woman. She made a dress out of the Navy bedspread, and here was the Navy insignia right on her butt. It fit just--just right. And but they--they really appreciated the donation of the clothing. And they even had some lepers. And that was part of our conversation as to what do we do with the lepers. Well, the lepers were put on the fo'c'sle right at the bow alongside the ramp. And they were able to keep them away from the rest of the people. Of course, we didn't want them getting with the crew either. So--but they--we got them out there and took them to the transport. And they went back home.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Would that still be in 1945 when you did that?

sp.speaker: George Harsch, Jr.
sp.p: Probably late '45 or early '46, in that time frame. Because I left there in June of '46. Yep. Yeah. That was a huge installation. And there--there was some other activity going on there, too. That place was just a mud hole. And they had brought some, two or three men over from the University of Hawaii. And they were agricultural people. And they were looking the islands over to see, of the natives for the island, what, what can they teach the natives on what to plant so that they, you know, would be self-sustaining. And they had all kinds of ideas on new methods for these people to get into. I brought home a samurai sword from there and a Japanese pistol. I had those as souvenirs for quite a while. But when our kids were born, boys are pretty curious, so I had the stuff tucked away up in the attic. But I know that they would explore, you know, looking for things. So I--that sword was so sharp. You know how you can feel a knife to feel if there's a sharp edge on it. If you would just feel that sharp edge you'd be cut. It was sharper than a razor. And so I sold the stuff. I didn't want the kids messing with that at all. And lots of times I regret that. But I don't know what problems I prevented by selling it. So. That's--that was just one other thing that I thought of.
